newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Dutch praise S.African search for reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Dutch praise S.African search for reconciliation.

text.p: The Netherlands on Thursday pledged moral and financial support for South Africa's search for post-apartheid reconciliation.

Speaking after a four-day state visit by Queen Beatrix, Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo told reporters the Dutch government was deeply impressed by what he called the brave search for reconciliation and forgiveness.
"Holland wants to give all moral and financial support on the road South Africa has chosen to walk... Whether it will succeed is something else," he said.

Van Mierlo said the Netherlands had reservations about the success of Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is empowered to probe the human rights record of white rule, to forgive perpetrators who confess and to compensate victims.
"My doubts would be far greater if it were not for the enormous moral authority of President (Nelson) Mandela," he said.
Van Mierlo said in response to questions that while the concerns were raised in private discussions, it was not for Queen Beatrix to express doubts in public.
"We have great admiration for the way these people follow the road they have choosen with all its uncertainty," he said.
Queen Beatrix rounded off her first state trip to South Africa with a visit to the Cape Town parliament in which apartheid was enacted and later dismantled.

Crown Prince Willem Alexander arrived from Johannesburg with his mother, but flew separately by helicopter to Robben Island in Table Bay, where Mandela spent 18 of his 27 years in jail for fighting white rule.
The queen's visit was the first by a Dutch monarch to the country that was ruled for more than 45 years by a Calvinist white minority of Dutch-descended Afrikaners.
Frene Ginwala, speaker of the South African parliament, showed Beatrix the national assembly in which Mandela was elected as the country's first black president in 1994.

Cyril Ramaphosa, secretary general of the ruling African National Congress, showed her the former whites-only chamber in which apartheid was enacted and in which Dutch-born prime minister Hendrik Verwoerd was assassinated by a lone fanatic in 1966.
The queen's programme for the day included museum visits and, at her own request, a seminar with Afrikaans-language writers.

Her final appointment before a private holiday in the country was a scheduled meeting with the Dutch community in the 17th century castle built by Dutch seaman Jan van Riebeeck, South Africa's first European settler.
